blocks.text: Start with the size of the home: ==350 square feet==, about 32 square metres, split into three tiny rooms in central Moscow. Four people lived there. Michael Brin, his wife Eugenia (everyone calls her Genia), Michael's mother Maya, and from August 21, 1973, a baby named Sergey. By Moscow standards this was not a bad deal. Many families in the city still shared communal flats with strangers.

The courtyard of the big five-storey block was Sergey's first playground. Russian tradition said a child needed fresh air, so he was sent out for two hours in the morning and two in the evening, in every season. Moscow winters did not count as an excuse.
A toddler outside in a Moscow January. Twice a day. Nobody thought it odd.
A father who kept hearing no

To understand Sergey you have to meet his father first. Michael wanted to be an astronomer. Officially, the Soviet Union had no anti-Semitism. In practice, Jews were shut out of the physics department at Moscow State University because leaders did not trust them near nuclear rocket research, and astronomy counted as physics. So the dream died before college even started.

He tried mathematics instead, and even that had a trap. Jewish applicants sat the Moscow State entrance exam in separate rooms and were graded more harshly. People called those rooms “gas chambers”. Michael got in with help from a well-connected family friend, and in 1970 he graduated with honours. Then the next door closed.
I had all A's except for three classes where I got B's: history of the Communist Party, military training and statistics. But nobody would even consider me for graduate school because I was Jewish.
blocks.who: Michael Brin, Sergey's father, to Moment magazine

blocks.text: He got a B in statistics. He later taught statistics at Maryland.

His day job became economist at GOSPLAN, the agency that planned the whole Soviet economy. His task, as he tells it, was to show that Russian living standards would soon beat America's. “And I proved it,” he told a reporter decades later. “I know enough about math to prove whatever you want.”
Remember this line the next time someone shows you a perfect spreadsheet.

At night he kept doing real mathematics. He sneaked into evening seminars at the university and wrote research papers. The system had one loophole: you could earn a doctorate without graduate school if you passed certain exams and an institution agreed to look at your thesis.

He needed an official adviser who was ethnically Russian and an unofficial Jewish mentor, because, in his words, “Jews could not have Jewish advisers.” That mentor was a mathematician named Anatole Katok. Remember the name.
Michael defended his thesis in Kharkov, Ukraine, and went straight back to GOSPLAN. The reward was a raise of ==100 rubles==. “I thought I was rich. Life was beautiful,” he said with a chuckle.

Genia had also fought through the entrance hurdles at Moscow State and worked in a research lab at the Soviet Oil and Gas Institute. She was happy there. “I was content in my job and had many friends,” she said. __So nobody in this family was starving. What they were running out of was a future.__
“We cannot stay here any more”

In the summer of 1977 Michael went to a maths conference in Warsaw. For the first time he could talk freely with colleagues from America, France, England and Germany. They were not monsters, he found.

They described the work and the comfort of life beyond the Iron Curtain. He came home and told his wife and mother: “We cannot stay here any more.” Sergey, not yet old enough to remember any of it, was about four.
Seeing the other side once was enough. Travel can end an old belief.
Genia said no. She had lived in Moscow all her life, she had a good job, and she had a small son. “I didn't want to go,” she recalled. “It took a while for me and his mother to agree.”
Michael had to do the convincing, and he admits he was thinking as much about his own future as his son's. For Genia the final answer came down to the boy. In her words, “it was 80/20 about Sergey.”
Big decisions are rarely unanimous. Someone has to keep arguing, kindly, for months.

Applying to leave was dangerous. Plenty of families became “refuseniks”: no visa, no work, stuck for years. Nobody had promised Michael a job abroad. They applied anyway in ==September 1978==, and he was fired at once.

Genia had got her job through a relative, and he begged her to get out quickly so he would not be punished. She could not tell her coworkers the real reason, so she invented a better job at a place that did not exist. “I made up—totally made up—the name of a place where I was planning to work,” she said.

For example: look at what that one form cost them. Two salaries gone, with no visa, no date and no job waiting. To get by, Michael translated technical books into English and started teaching himself computer programming, because he did not expect any university to hire him if they ever got out. Genia found temporary work, again lying about her situation. The two of them took turns looking after five-year-old Sergey at home, instead of sending him to a Soviet pre-school.

Then they waited, and for many Soviet Jews the papers never came at all. The Brins got theirs in ==May 1979==. “We hoped it would happen,” Genia said, “but we were completely surprised by how quickly it did.” They were among the last Jews allowed out until the Gorbachev era.
__The door they walked through was about to shut for years. Hard work got them to the door. Luck held it open.__
Vienna, Paris, and a 1973 Ford Maverick

Sergey turned six that summer. All he remembers of the journey is that it was “unsettling”. “We were in different places from day to day,” he said. In Vienna the family was met by the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society, known as HIAS.

It handled their papers and bought their tickets. There was also a real question to settle: Israel or America? “We, after a prolonged decision, chose the States,” Genia said years later. Science magazine later pointed out there is no way of knowing what would have happened otherwise.
Science magazine later asked it seriously: might Google have been Israeli?

Next came the suburbs of Paris. Anatole Katok, Michael's old unofficial mentor, had left Russia a year earlier. He arranged a temporary research post for Michael at the Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, and he helped open the way to a teaching job at the University of Maryland. A quiet favour from a teacher moved the whole family across an ocean.

They landed at New York's Kennedy Airport on ==October 25, 1979==. Friends from Moscow picked them up. Sergey's first memory of America is the back seat of that car, staring at the giant automobiles on the highway as they drove to Long Island.

In Maryland they rented a plain cinder-block house in a lower-middle-class neighbourhood near the campus. A ==$2,000== loan from the local Jewish community bought them a 1973 Ford Maverick. A synagogue in Greenbelt, Mishkan Torah, helped them find furniture. Michael would go on to teach at Maryland for decades, and Genia became a research scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. In 1979, though, they were two immigrants with a borrowed car.

Michael's raise for earning a Ph.D. the hard way
Community loan that bought the family's first car
Sergey's age when he reached America

blocks.text: That money shortage stayed in him. By the time a magazine reporter called him, he was worth billions and he still shopped at Costco. He had even bought his parents a membership.
From my parents, I certainly learned to be frugal and to be happy without very many things. It's interesting—I still find myself not wanting to leave anything on the plate uneaten.
The boy nobody thought was special

On Katok's advice, the Brins sent Sergey to Paint Branch Montessori School in Adelphi, Maryland. It was the closest private school, and they hoped it would ease him into a new language and new friends. His English was basic and his accent heavy. “It was a difficult year for him, the first year,” Genia said.
They had been told children are like sponges, “and that wasn't the case.” Language did not come naturally to him. Numbers did.

The school's director, Patty Barshay, became a friend to the whole family. That first December she invited them to her Christmas Day party, which she described as “a bunch of Jewish people with nothing to do on Christmas Day”. She also taught Genia to drive. When the Brins had her over for dinner she asked what kind of meat was on the table, and Genia did not know. They had never seen so much meat in one place as American supermarkets offered.
Imagine a supermarket as culture shock. That is how far they had come.
Montessori classrooms let children choose their own work. Sergey went for puzzles, maps and maths games that taught multiplication. “I could grow at my own pace,” he said later.

He stayed from age six to eleven. And here is the part worth remembering: Barshay liked him and was proud of him, but she never saw a genius coming. “He was interested in everything,” she said, then added: “I never thought he was any brighter than anyone else.”
His own head teacher didn't spot it. Remember that when nobody spots you.

__What that school gave him was not praise. It was permission to follow his own questions.__ His mother said it later in plainer words: the method gave him “a basis for independent thinking and a hands-on approach to life.” Outside that classroom, things were less gentle. “As a child, I had an accent,” Sergey said. “I came to the U.S. at the age of six, and so I was teased and stuff in elementary school.”

The worst of it came at Hebrew school. He went to Mishkan Torah for the better part of three years and hated the language lessons and everything else. “He was teased there by other kids and he begged us not to send him any more,” his mother remembered. “Eventually, it worked.”
At home, his father was a dry-humoured presence. “Sergey was a good boy,” Michael once joked, “when he was asleep.”

photo.caption: A Commodore 64, the home computer Sergey's parents gave him when he was nine.
photo.author: Evan-Amos

blocks.text: The computer arrived at nine. His school had an Apple II, and then, as he tells it, “When I was 9, my parents gave me a Commodore 64, which was fun.” He has said it was easier to program your own machine back then than it is now, because today's computers hide so much complexity. Michael did not sit him down for lessons. “I didn't systematically teach Sergey; he would ask when he wanted to know something,” his father recalled.
No tutor. No coding class. A machine, and a father who answered questions.

At eleven he made one more choice of his own. A three-week family trip to Israel stirred his interest in being Jewish, so his parents asked another synagogue about preparing him for a bar mitzvah. The rabbi said catching up would take more than a year. Sergey did not want to wait past his thirteenth birthday, so he dropped the idea. Even then, he was not willing to wait around.

blocks.text: Jump forward thirty years to the day. On ==October 25, 2009==, Sergey announced a $1 million gift to HIAS, the group that had met his family in Vienna. He had been asking his parents which organisations they owed thanks to, and his mother told him about it. She also served on its board. “I would have never had the kinds of opportunities I've had here in the Soviet Union, or even in Russia today,” he told The New York Times.

So here is what the first twelve years hand him. A father who refused to accept the answer he was given. A mother who gave up a life she liked, mostly for her son's sake. A slowly dawning lesson in what happens when one authority controls who may learn what. __Long before he took a risk of his own, he had lived inside his parents' risk, with no income and no guarantee.__

Ask Sergey about his teenage years and he does not tell a story about fitting in. He once listed the reasons he felt like an outsider: being Jewish, especially in Russia; being an immigrant in America; and being so far ahead in maths that he was always the youngest in the class. He summed it up in a sentence.
I never felt like a part of the majority.
blocks.who: Sergey Brin, quoted in The Jewish Chronicle

blocks.text: He has never claimed to be the popular kid. “I don't regard myself as being really popular going through school,” he told an interviewer at 27, “but that was never that important to me, and I always had friends.” One of those friends turns out to matter a lot in this chapter.
Not popular. Didn't care much. Kept a few real friends. That's enough.
A house where degrees were the only religion

The Brins were not very observant. “We felt our Jewishness in different ways, not by keeping kosher or going to synagogue,” Michael said. The one value the family held without argument was scholarship. In 1987, when Sergey was 13 or 14, his brother Sam was born, and Sam later became the family's favourite proof of how far this went.
As a boy who loved basketball more than homework, he asked his father: “Is it true that before you play in the N.B.A. you have to get a Ph.D.?” His father couldn't resist. “Yes, Sam, that's it!”
In this house, even the basketball joke needed a Ph.D.
By middle school, Sergey was already known as a maths prodigy. That word gets thrown around cheaply, so look at what he actually did with his spare time. He messed about on a friend's computer.

“I remember in middle school, a very good friend — who I'm still in touch with — he had a Macintosh, one of the early ones,” he said. The two of them would just sit and program. They built little artificial intelligence experiments, including a program that talked back to you. They wrote one that simulated gravity.
“It was just for fun, and purely out of intellectual curiosity,” he said. “I have to admit I was a bit of a nerd. I still am.”

For example: take the third project he mentioned. The two boys tried to write a program that could look at printed letters and work out what they said. Today that is called optical character recognition, or OCR. Asked when he first felt the power of computers, he pointed to these sessions. No marks, no customer and no competition, just two kids and an early Macintosh.
Middle school. Nobody asked him to build any of this. Read that twice.

__Look at the pattern: gravity, speech, reading. He picked problems because they were hard and interesting, not because they were useful yet.__ Years later he said what drew him in was the power computers gave you, and the idea that you could use it to make something useful “beyond video games and things like that.”

What did he read? He remembers enjoying the autobiographical books of the physicist Richard Feynman, though he did not say exactly when. One passage stuck with him: Feynman explaining that he wanted to be “a Leonardo, an artist and a scientist.” Sergey found that “pretty inspiring”. “It seemed like a very great life he led,” he said.
Three years of high school, and not one more

photo.caption: Eleanor Roosevelt High School in Greenbelt, Maryland, seen from the back. Sergey raced through in three years.
photo.author: Truco 503

blocks.text: After Montessori came the shock of ordinary school. Eleanor Roosevelt High School in Greenbelt was a large public school, and Sergey went through it in ==three years==, stacking up a year's worth of college credits on the way. The Los Angeles Times, reporting on a talk he gave in 2009, said he felt stuck in a 19th-century curriculum after leaving Montessori. That is the paper's summary, but the frustration is clear.

According to some accounts, he was also cocky about it. Biographer Janet Lowe writes that he often challenged his teachers on their methods and their results. Being right is one thing. Telling the teacher so is another. Later a Stanford professor would use the word “brash” for the same streak.
Being right in class is easy. Being right kindly takes years longer.

Lowe also writes that he began studying maths at the University of Maryland at 15, where his father taught. Whether he formally graduated is where sources split. The Los Angeles Times and Lowe say he quit high school after his junior year, and Wired says he left a year early. The Academy of Achievement says he graduated in 1990. Either way he was done with high school by 16, and in college by 17.

Here is something this book promised to be honest about. If you came to this chapter for the teenage hustle, the paper round or the first small business, we could not find one. Nothing reliable says he sold anything or started anything as a teenager.

His father told a reporter flatly: “He did not learn it from us, absolutely not our area.” __Some founders start selling at 12. This one spent his teens learning to do hard things well and, as far as the record shows, sold nothing until his twenties.__
No teen side hustle here. Skills first, money later. Both routes can work.
June 1990: the sixteen-year-old and the supercomputer

Now for the detail almost nobody tells. It sits in Sergey's own résumé, typed up at Stanford in January 1996 and still online. The first job he lists starts in ==June 1990==, two months before his seventeenth birthday, at the University of Maryland Institute for Advanced Computer Studies. He writes that he developed parallel algorithms for image processing, including smoothing and enhancing pictures, and parallel 3-D graphics routines “suitable for a flight simulator.”

The machine is the wow. He wrote that code for “a Connection Machine 2 with 16384 processors.” Ordinary computers of that time worked through instructions one after another. The Connection Machine split a job across thousands of tiny processors working all at once.

Its maker, Thinking Machines, launched the CM-2 in 1987 and called it the world's fastest computer, with a top version of about 64,000 processors. UPI reported a price of ==$1 million to $6 million==. Maryland's machine was the smaller 16K size, so its own price was presumably lower. We could not find the exact figure.

photo.caption: A Connection Machine CM-2 at the Computer History Museum. Sergey programmed this model at 16.
photo.author: Kevin

blocks.text: He was sixteen. Sixteen. Writing flight-simulator graphics on a supercomputer.

blocks.text: His résumé does not say how he got that job, whether it paid, or who hired him. His father taught at the same university, so the campus was hardly a strange place. __Being near a serious university gave a curious kid access to machines most adults never touched.__ You may not have a father on the faculty. But the move is copyable: find the nearest lab doing something hard, and ask to help.
Pebbles at a police car

That same summer, Sergey went back. In 1990 Michael was leading a group of gifted high school maths students on a two-week exchange to the Soviet Union, and he took the whole family despite real unease about how the authorities would treat them. It also meant seeing relatives in Moscow, including Sergey's grandfather, another Ph.D. mathematician. Sergey was weeks away from turning 17, going back to the country he had left at six.

The Soviet empire was falling apart in front of him. On the second day the group toured a sanitarium in the countryside near Moscow. Sergey took his father aside, looked him in the eye, and said: “Thank you for taking us all out of Russia.”

It is one of the most quoted lines of his life, and his father's reaction is better. “There were only two occasions when my children were grateful to me,” Michael said dryly. The other one, he explained, involved Sam and a broken toilet.
Two thank-yous in a lifetime. One for a country, one for a toilet.

Genia, sitting beside him during that interview, protested at once. “Misha, what are you talking about!?” she said. She often did that when their memories differed. Arguing over the facts seems to be how this family talks.

The trip brought out something else too. Sergey says it woke up his childhood fear of authority, and he dealt with the fear the way a 16-year-old might. His impulse was to throw pebbles at a police car.

Two officers got out, “quite upset”. His parents managed to calm things down. Imagine that scene for a moment: an immigrant family back in Moscow on a sensitive trip, and the teenage son throws pebbles at the police.
My rebelliousness, I think, came out of being born in Moscow. I'd say this is something that followed me into adulthood.
Dislike of authority has a source. For him it was a whole country.

He came home, and in September 1990 he started full time at the University of Maryland. He was 17. Asked as an adult whether being the son of Russian immigrants had held him back, he answered the opposite. “I think, if anything, I feel like I have gotten a gift by being in the States rather than growing up in Russia,” he said. __A kid who has seen the other version of his own life does not take his chances for granted.__

Most people read the Sergey Brin story as a jump straight from clever kid to Stanford to Google. His own 1996 résumé shows something else: a long run of real work started before he could vote. It is worth reading slowly, because almost nobody does.
Five jobs by twenty

items.text: University of Maryland computing institute: parallel image processing and 3-D graphics on a Connection Machine.
General Electric Information Services: a macro language library in C++.
Maryland maths department, with Dr. Goldman: a C++ library to visualise objects in non-Euclidean geometries.
Back at GE: a graphical front end for a file transfer program.
Maryland Systems Design and Analysis Group: scheduling algorithms for real-time systems.
Graduates at 19 in maths and computer science, with high honours in maths.
Wolfram Research: a code analysis tool for the Mathematica source code.
Starts at Stanford, weeks after turning 20.

blocks.text: Look at one line from the GE job. He did it at 17, the summer he turned 18. He writes that the library he built “was important for GEIS because it demonstrated the use of C++ to them.” So a teenager on a summer job was demonstrating C++ to a General Electric division. He writes about it like a professional, and he explains the value to the business and not just the code.
He was 17. Explain your work by what it changed. Copy this habit.

The Wolfram summer has its own footnote. Stephen Wolfram, the founder, later said his company had once planned to split the language inside Mathematica into its own product, called the M Language. “And we even had people working on it, like Sergey Brin when he was an intern with us in 1993,” he said. The plan faded. Wolfram went back to the idea many years later and released it as the Wolfram Language.

For example: count the different kinds of problem he had touched by 19. Picture smoothing on a supercomputer. Flight-simulator graphics. Strange geometry where parallel lines behave oddly. Finding good-enough answers to NP-complete scheduling problems, the kind no known method solves quickly. Tools for reading other people's code. That is five different fields before most people pick a major.

We looked for what these jobs paid and found nothing reliable. It does not matter much. __He was not collecting money yet. He was collecting hard problems, and each one taught him something the next one needed.__ When he finished at Maryland he graduated near the top of his class, and he won a prestigious National Science Foundation fellowship for graduate school.

MIT turned him down. He insisted on Stanford anyway, for the beautiful campus and the weather, and because he knew the place had a reputation for backing high-tech entrepreneurs. Even so, his mind was on finishing a doctorate, not on starting a business. One month before leaving, he realised he could not cook, so he taught himself. His house speciality became Chernobyl Chili, which he described as “45 minutes in the microwave.”
MIT said no. Think about that the next time a rejection arrives.
The goof-off who passed everything

He reached Stanford in September 1993, just past 20. Steven Levy, in his book In the Plex, calls him one of the youngest students ever to start the program. “He skipped a million years,” said Craig Silverstein, who arrived a year later.
Soon after arriving he cleared all the tests required for a doctorate. That left him free to sample whatever he liked until a thesis topic turned up. It did not turn up for a long time.

He loaded up on sailing, swimming and scuba diving. He told a writer that the weather was just too good. He tried gymnastics, skiing, rollerblading, even the flying trapeze. His father noticed. “I asked him if he was taking any advanced courses, and he said, ‘yes, advanced swimming,’” Michael remembered.

He had a habit of bursting into professors' offices without knocking. One adviser, Rajeev Motwani, recalled: “He was the brash young man. But he was so smart, it just oozed out of him.” Moment magazine, which liked him, still described a self-assurance that at times spilled over into arrogance. The school's own history records that he rollerbladed through the Gates Building hallways, and that he renumbered its offices so the numbers showed the distance between rooms.

photo.caption: Stanford's Gates Computer Science Building, whose hallways Sergey rollerbladed and whose offices he helped number.
photo.author: Frank Schulenburg

blocks.text: Renumbering a building for fun. That is what “obsessed with efficiency” looks like.
Under the goofing, the work was serious. By August 1995 he had a master's degree. Two papers had come out that year. One was a solo paper on searching huge sets of data for close matches.

The other, with his adviser Hector Garcia-Molina and fellow student James Davis, was COPS: the COpyright Protection System, for catching illegally copied documents automatically. Years later, Google itself would be fighting copyright lawsuits. Levy reports that Garcia-Molina, who had seen plenty of bright students, said simply: “He was brilliant.”

Then there were the side projects, which his résumé cheerfully files under “Current Research Directions and Hacks”. In January 1996 he had just started a system for personal movie ratings. “You rate the movies you have seen,” he wrote. The program would then find people with similar taste and predict what else you would like.

Today we would call that a recommendation engine. He wrote it in Python. He also wrote his own tool to turn LaTeX science papers into web pages, because he found the existing ones “a little frustrating”.

For example: his Stanford home page is still online, and it reads like a graduate student having fun. It lists how to reach him by email, post and phone, and next to “GPS” it says “Working on it.” It points to his parents' pages and to his little brother's elementary school. Near the top, one short line records the end of this story: “Currently I am at Google.”

The most important person in those years did not even hold the title. “Officially, Rajeev was not my advisor,” Sergey wrote after Motwani's death in 2009, “and yet he played just as big a role in my research, education, and professional development.” When Sergey got interested in data mining, Motwani helped organise a regular meeting group on it, which became known as MIDAS.

“Even though I was just one of hundreds of graduate students in the department, he always made the time and effort to help,” Sergey wrote. __Find the person whose door is open. It is often not the person on the form.__
Very important: your most useful mentor may not hold the official title.
The tour guide and the guy from Michigan

In 1995 Sergey volunteered to show accepted students around, including a walk through San Francisco. A University of Michigan engineer named Larry Page ended up in his group. They spent the day going up and down the hills fighting about things like urban planning. “I thought he was pretty obnoxious,” Page said. “He had really strong opinions about things, and I guess I did, too.”
We both found each other obnoxious. But we say it a little bit jokingly.
blocks.who: Sergey Brin, in John Battelle's account for Wired

blocks.text: Page arrived that fall and began looking at the links between web pages, with a project he called BackRub. Sergey had wandered from group to group without settling on a thesis. He joined because of the data: Page was pulling in huge amounts of it, and that was exactly what a data miner wants. Asked later why he chose this one, he said “this was the most exciting project, both because it tackled the Web, which represents human knowledge, and because I liked Larry.”
“Because I liked Larry.” That was half his reason. Choose your co-founder carefully.

Friends soon treated them as one person, “LarryandSergey”. Page came up with the idea of treating links like citations in research papers, and Sergey brought the maths to rank pages by who linked to them. __Neither of them could have done it alone, and they never stopped arguing.__ The next chapters cover how that worked in detail. What matters here is how scrappy it was.

They had no budget, so they begged. “At Stanford we'd stand on the loading dock and try to snag computers as they came in,” Page recalled. They would see who had received 20 machines and ask for one. Page's dorm room became the machine room and Sergey's became the office.

Their original server held ten 4-gigabyte drives, encased in toy building blocks. The crawler at one point ate nearly half of Stanford's network bandwidth, and in fall 1996 it kept knocking the university offline. Two other students, Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg, were “critical” to the work, as the founders themselves wrote.

items.label: Searches a day while still at Stanford
Storage in the original toy-brick server
Stanford's bandwidth used at one point by their crawler

blocks.text: The first version of Google went up on the Stanford website in August 1996, a year after they met. The domain google.com was registered on September 15, 1997. Levy says Sergey designed the playful early logo himself, using an open-source graphics program.

There is a strange side story that gets twisted online, so here it is straight. The research in their 1998 paper was funded through a federal digital library project backed by the NSF, DARPA and NASA. A separate intelligence-community programme, called MDDS, also funded work at Stanford. Its manager, Bhavani Thuraisingham, recalled visits where “Mr. Brin would rush in on roller blades, give his presentation and rush out.” She later corrected her account to say plainly: “MDDS never funded Google; it funded Stanford University.”

In 1998 the two of them published the paper that explained the whole thing. Near the end they added an appendix on what they called “Advertising and Mixed Motives”, and it contains a line every student of Google should know. Two years later, in October 2000, Google launched AdWords.
we expect that advertising funded search engines will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers.
blocks.who: Sergey Brin and Lawrence Page, The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine, 1998

blocks.text: Read this twice. Then ask what changes your mind once money arrives.
“We tried as hard as we could to avoid doing that”

Here is the part that surprises people. They did not want to start a company. “For three years, we tried as hard as we could to avoid doing that,” Sergey said in 2000. Of Stanford, he added, “we were pretty comfortable” there.

Page, whose father had died during his first year there, saw finishing the Ph.D. as something of a tribute to him. Sergey, raised by academics, did not want to leave either. In his family, a doctorate was simply what you did.

So they tried to sell. They offered the technology around for ==$1 million==, and no one wanted it, because everyone believed the money was in portals such as Yahoo and AOL. Yahoo's David Filo, a friend, told them to build it themselves.

“When it's fully developed and scalable,” he told them, “let's talk again.” Another portal boss was blunter, according to Google's own early history: “As long as we're 80 percent as good as our competitors, that's good enough. Our users don't really care about search.”
Their worst decision was offering to sell. Luckily, the buyers made a worse one.

__Had anyone said yes, the whole thing would have gone for $1 million.__ Moment put Google's value at $150 billion by early 2007. That rejection may be the most valuable thing that ever happened to them. Take that thought seriously the next time a big company passes on your idea.

Then came a nudge from down the hall. David Cheriton, a Stanford professor who had never taught or advised either of them, had just sold a startup. They went to him for advice about licensing and raising money. He told them, “If you have a baby, you need to raise it.” And he added something every first-time founder needs tattooed somewhere: “Raising the money isn't the hard part–building the company is.”

What actually pushed them was computers. They had been borrowing machines from all over the department, and it was getting out of hand. So they made the choice that turned a research project into a business, and they made it with credit cards.
“We spent about $15,000 on a terabyte [a million megabytes] of disks,” Sergey said. “We spread that across three credit cards.” Only after that did they sit down and write a business plan.

For example: picture two doctoral students in the first half of 1998. They have no company, no customers and no investors, and $15,000 of disks on three credit cards. Google's own early history says the cards were maxed out. Their ranking method works better than anything on the market, and the market has told them it does not care. That is what the start of something big looks like up close. It looks like a bad idea.

Their parents were not cheering. “We were definitely upset,” Genia said. “We thought everybody in their right mind ought to get a Ph.D.” Sergey remembers a conversation with his adviser, who told him: “Look, if this Google thing pans out, then great. If not, you can return to graduate school and finish your thesis.”
Sergey chuckled when he retold it. “I said, ‘Yeah, OK, why not? I'll just give it a try.’”
Not “bet everything”. He kept a way back. Smart founders usually do.
A cheque for a company that didn't exist

In August 1998, Cheriton set up a meeting on his own front porch in Palo Alto with his old business partner Andy Bechtolsheim, a co-founder of Sun Microsystems. It was very early in the morning. They showed the search engine outdoors, on the porch, and Bechtolsheim was in a hurry. “He had to run off somewhere,” Sergey said, “so he said, instead of us discussing all the details, why don't I just write you a check?”

As Cheriton remembers it, Bechtolsheim ran to his car for his chequebook. The cheque was for ==$100,000== and made out to “Google Inc.” There was just one problem. No such company existed, and the two of them did not even have a bank account.

“Well when you do, stick it in there,” Bechtolsheim told them. It sat in Page's desk drawer for a couple of weeks while they scrambled to form a corporation. Cheriton put in money too, some $200,000 by the Stanford Daily's count. By the time they closed the round they had raised almost $1 million.

blocks.text: Google filed for incorporation in California on September 4, 1998, and opened for business on September 7, in a rented garage in Menlo Park belonging to Susan Wojcicki, a friend who needed help with her mortgage. They paid a reported $1,700 a month. Google's early history lists the perks: a washer and dryer and a hot tub. It had a staff of three, including its first hire, fellow student Craig Silverstein, and it was already answering 10,000 searches a day.

Even then they kept one foot at Stanford. That fall Sergey and Larry co-taught a class there, CS 349, on data mining, search and the web, and gave students access to the pages they had collected. The University of Maryland's alumni page still describes him as on leave from the Ph.D. program, and we found no report that he ever went back. He kept that door open and never needed it.

blocks.text: So here he is at 25. Refugee, former school outsider, supercomputer programmer at 16, unfinished Ph.D., three credit cards, one garage. __It all looks random until you see the thread: he kept walking toward the hardest interesting problem nearby.__ What comes next is the company.

factCheck.method: Family and childhood scenes rest mainly on Mark Malseed's Moment profile, built on his interviews with Sergey, Michael and Genia Brin and Patty Barshay, cross-checked against Lowe, The Economist and The Jewish Chronicle. Early work comes from Brin's own 1996 résumé and Stanford home page (primary), with Wolfram's own account confirming the 1993 internship. The Stanford and founding period uses Wired (Battelle), Stanford Engineering's history, MIT Technology Review's 2000 interview, The Stanford Daily and Google's own archived histories. Quotes were checked against the page text at time of writing. Levy's In the Plex was read as book text, and only claims stated there are attributed to it.

disputed.claim: When Brin and Page first met in 1995
disputed.note: Moment and one passage of Stanford Engineering's history say spring 1995 (a prospective-student weekend). Wired, The Guardian, Levy and another passage of the same Stanford history say summer 1995. The text says only '1995'. Google's own early history also gives conflicting ages for them at the meeting (21/22 in the 2011 version, 23/24 in the 2005 version), so ages at that meeting are not stated.

disputed.claim: Whether Brin graduated from high school
disputed.note: Academy of Achievement says he graduated from Eleanor Roosevelt High School in 1990. The Los Angeles Times and Lowe say he quit after his junior year. Wired says he left a year early. Moment says he 'raced through in three years'. All agree on three years and on entering Maryland full time in 1990, which the résumé confirms. The text presents the split.

disputed.claim: Brin began studying at the University of Maryland at 15
disputed.note: Stated by Lowe only. His résumé lists Maryland study from September 1990, when he was 17, and his first Maryland job from June 1990. Attributed to Lowe in the text.

Google's 2011 history, The Guardian and CNBC say it filed on September 4, 1998. Wired's 'This Day' piece and Stanford Engineering say incorporated on September 7. Google's 2005 history says it opened its door on September 7. The text uses Sept 4 for filing and Sept 7 for opening.

disputed.claim: How long the Bechtolsheim cheque waited
disputed.note: Moment says two weeks, Google's 2005 history says a couple of weeks, other retellings say about a month. The text says a couple of weeks.
The Stanford Daily says some $200,000. Other accounts say he matched Bechtolsheim's $100,000. Attributed to the Stanford Daily in the text; exact sum not confirmed in filings.

Moment says the family applied in September 1978 and received papers in May 1979. J. Weekly says the visa was granted in 1978 and JTA's text says the family left in 1976. Moment's dated account, from the parents themselves, is used. HIAS and NYT confirm the Oct 25, 1979 arrival.

In the Plex says Brin was four when his family emigrated and nineteen on arrival at Stanford. Moment, NYT, Wired and others say six at emigration. His résumé (Sept 1993) and birth date (Aug 21, 1973) make him just 20 at Stanford. The text uses six and 20.
Lowe says his father. Brin himself says 'my parents' in the Los Angeles Times. The text uses his own words.

disputed.claim: Hours spent outdoors as a toddler
disputed.note: Moment's wording: two hours in the morning and evening each day. Lowe condenses this to two hours a day. The text follows Moment, read as two hours each time; the source wording allows either reading.

disputed.claim: US intelligence (MDDS) funding of Brin's Stanford work
disputed.note: Quartz (2017) says MDDS and a DARPA-NSF grant funded research by Brin and Page. Bhavani Thuraisingham's original 2013 article said Brin was partly funded; her January 2015 correction removed that, says MDDS funded Stanford and never Google, and reports Google's statement that Brin did not work on Query Flocks. The 1998 Anatomy paper's acknowledgements name only the NSF-led Digital Library project. The text states this and draws no conclusion beyond the correction.
Levy says Sergey made it using GIMP. Levy is the only source used for this, and the text attributes it to him.
